questions.question_text:
A population satisfies $\dfrac{dP}{dt}=0.006P(250-P)$.
Written in the form $kP\left(1-\dfrac{P}{C}\right)$, what are $C$ and $k$?

options.why: Read the coefficient straight off without multiplying it by $250$ to convert to the bracket form.
Swapped the two results, using the growth constant as the capacity.
Swapped the roles of the coefficient and the capacity without converting the form at all.
Missed the factor $P$, so the extinct population $P=0$ was left out.
Used half the carrying capacity, which is where growth is fastest, not where it stops.
Included half the carrying capacity as well; at $P=360$ the rate is a maximum, not zero.
Left the exponent positive, which makes the population fall towards zero instead of rising towards $600$.
Used $\frac{C}{P_{0}}$ instead of $\frac{C-P_{0}}{P_{0}}$ when evaluating the constant.
Used $\frac{C}{P_{0}}$ for the constant and also left the exponent positive.

questions.question_text:
A population is modelled by $N=\dfrac{3200}{1+7e^{-0.5t}}$, with $t$ in years.
Find $N(8)$, correct to the nearest whole number.

options.why: Gave the carrying capacity, which the model approaches but never reaches at a finite time.
Evaluated the model at $t=0$ instead of $t=8$.
Gave half the carrying capacity, which is where growth is fastest, not the value at $t=8$.

questions.question_text:
A population satisfies $\dfrac{dP}{dt}=0.24P\left(1-\dfrac{P}{5000}\right)$.
Which explanation shows, without calculus, why its rate of increase is greatest at $P=2500$?

options.text: The rate is a concave down quadratic in $P$ with roots $0$ and $5000$, so its maximum lies halfway between the roots.
The rate is directly proportional to $P$, so it is greatest halfway to the carrying capacity.
options.why: Ignored the factor $1-\frac{P}{5000}$; direct proportionality alone would not give a maximum at half capacity.

options.text: The bracket is zero at $P=2500$, so the rate is greatest there.
options.why: Treated a zero rate as a maximum and incorrectly placed the bracket's zero at half capacity rather than $P=5000$.

options.text: The rate is a concave up quadratic in $P$, so its greatest value lies halfway between its roots.
options.why: Reversed the sign of the quadratic coefficient; a concave up quadratic has a minimum halfway between its roots.

questions.solution_text:
$\dfrac{dP}{dt}=0.24P\left(1-\dfrac{P}{5000}\right)$ is a concave down quadratic in $P$ with roots $0$ and $5000$.
Its maximum is halfway between the roots, at $P=2500$.

questions.question_text:
A population satisfies $\dfrac{dP}{dt}=\dfrac{1}{8}P\left(1-\dfrac{P}{700}\right)$ with $P(0)=950$.
Which statement describes the long-term behaviour of $P$?

options.text: $P$ decreases and approaches $700$ from above, never reaching it at a finite time.
$P$ increases without bound, because the growth constant $\frac{1}{8}$ is positive.
options.why: Reads the sign of $k$ alone; with $P>700$ the bracket is negative, so the rate is negative.

options.text: $P$ decreases to zero, because the population started above the carrying capacity.
options.why: Overshoots the constant solution $P=700$, which a solution curve cannot cross.

options.text: $P$ stays at $950$, because that is the initial population and the model is at equilibrium.
options.why: Treats any initial value as an equilibrium; only $P=0$ and $P=700$ make the rate zero.

questions.solution_text:
$1-\dfrac{950}{700}<0$, so $\dfrac{dP}{dt}<0$ and $P$ decreases.
$P=700$ is a constant solution, so the curve cannot cross it.
$P$ falls towards $700$ from above and approaches it without reaching it.

questions.question_text:
A population is modelled by $P=\dfrac{400}{1+3e^{-0.4t}}$, with $t$ in years.
What are the initial population and the limiting population?

options.why: Swapped the value at $t=0$ and the limit as $t\to\infty$.
Used $e^{0.4t}$ in place of $e^{-0.4t}$ when taking the limit, making the denominator increase without bound.
Used half the carrying capacity as the initial population instead of substituting $t=0$.

questions.solution_text:
$P(0)=\dfrac{400}{1+3}=100$.
As $t\to\infty$, $e^{-0.4t}\to 0$, so $P\to 400$.
The initial population is $100$ and the limiting population is $400$.

questions.question_text:
A population satisfies $\dfrac{dP}{dt}=kP\left(1-\dfrac{P}{2400}\right)$ with $P(0)=400$ and $P(5)=1200$, where $t$ is in years.
Using $\dfrac{2400}{P(2400-P)}=\dfrac{1}{P}+\dfrac{1}{2400-P}$, derive the population formula and find $P(10)$.

options.why: Assumed the population keeps tripling, using $1200\times 3$, which ignores the carrying capacity.
Assumed the population has reached the carrying capacity, which it approaches but never attains.
Used $e^{-10k}=\frac{1}{10}$, halving the exponent's effect instead of squaring $e^{-5k}$.
